questions.title: Neutrophil nuclear shape
questions.question: Neutrophil nucleus is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A single unlobed nucleus describes a monocyte or a lymphocyte, not a neutrophil.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A bilobed nucleus is the eosinophil's (and, less obviously, the basophil's) identifying feature, not the neutrophil's.
explanations.C: Correct. The neutrophil's single nucleus is divided into three to five lobes joined by thin chromatin strands, giving it its "polymorphonuclear" name. This multilobed shape is the fastest way to identify a neutrophil on a blood film, distinguishing it from the bilobed eosinophil and basophil and the rounded nuclei of monocytes and lymphocytes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Multilobed is one of the listed options, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that the neutrophil's nucleus is multilobed (3-5 lobes).

questions.title: Reticulocyte features, EXCEPT
questions.question: All are true for reticulocytes EXCEPT:

options.D: Reticulocytosis occurs in haemorrhage or high altitude

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). A reticulocyte is by definition the immature stage between the last nucleated erythroblast and the mature erythrocyte.
explanations.B: Correct — this is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Reticulocytes normally make up about 1% (not about 10%) of the total circulating erythrocyte count. A count near 10% would itself represent a marked reticulocytosis, not the resting baseline this option implies, so it is the one statement here that is not true of a normal reticulocyte count.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Like the mature erythrocyte, the reticulocyte has already lost its nucleus by the time it enters circulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Haemorrhage and high altitude both drive an appropriately increased marrow output of reticulocytes, i.e. reticulocytosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that reticulocytes normally make up about 1% of total erythrocytes, not about 10%.

questions.title: Erythrocyte structural adaptations
questions.question: Regarding adaptation of erythrocytes:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own — true, but not the fullest answer. Losing the nucleus and organelles is one real adaptation (it frees up room for haemoglobin), but the question asks for all adaptations at once.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own — true, but not the fullest answer. The biconcave disc shape increases the erythrocyte's surface area relative to its volume, but it is only one of the listed adaptations.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own — true, but not the fullest answer. A flexible membrane lets the erythrocyte deform to pass through capillaries narrower than its own resting diameter, but it too is only one adaptation.
explanations.D: Correct. All three are genuine, independently examinable adaptations of the mature erythrocyte: it has no nucleus or organelles, giving it more room for haemoglobin; it is shaped as a biconcave disc, which increases its surface-area-to-volume ratio for gas exchange; and its membrane is flexible enough to deform through capillaries narrower than the cell's own resting diameter. Together they explain how a cell built purely to carry oxygen is also built to survive squeezing through the smallest vessels in the body.

questions.learning_objective: List the erythrocyte's three structural adaptations: anucleate/organelle-free, biconcave shape, flexible membrane.

questions.title: Erythrocyte circulating lifespan
questions.question: The life span of an erythrocyte in the circulation is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 20 days is far shorter than an erythrocyte's true circulating lifespan.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 1 year overstates the true circulating lifespan by roughly a factor of three.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 5 weeks (about 35 days) is still well short of the true figure.
explanations.D: Correct. An average circulating erythrocyte survives about 120 days, which rounds to roughly 4 months. Aged erythrocytes are removed mainly by splenic and hepatic macrophages once their membrane deformability declines below the threshold needed to keep passing through splenic sinusoids, and the marrow replaces the lost cells at a matched rate under normal conditions.

questions.learning_objective: State that average circulating RBC lifespan is about 120 days (~4 months).

questions.title: Granules with a crystalline core
questions.question: Specific granules of these cells have crystalline core:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neutrophil specific granules carry antimicrobial enzymes and stain neutrally; they have no crystalline core.
explanations.B: Correct. The eosinophil's coarse, acidophilic specific granules contain major basic protein packed into a dense crystalline core, visible by electron microscopy inside a less-dense surrounding matrix. This crystalline-core structure is unique among the granulocytes to the eosinophil, and is what suits its granule contents to killing large parasites such as helminths that are too big to be phagocytosed outright.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Basophil specific granules carry histamine and heparin and are coarse and metachromatic, but they do not show a crystalline core.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Monocytes are agranular — they carry no specific granules at all, crystalline or otherwise.

questions.learning_objective: State that only the eosinophil's specific granules have a crystalline core.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IHI-103 > Blood and Hemopoiesis > Granulocyte identification

questions.title: How granular leukocytes differ
questions.question: Granular leukocytes differ in:

options.C: Staining reaction of their specific granules

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own — true, but not the fullest answer. Nuclear shape (multilobed, bilobed, or bilobed/obscured) is one real distinguishing feature, but not the only one asked for here.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own — true, but not the fullest answer. Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils do occur at very different relative percentages of the total leukocyte count, but that is only one of the listed criteria.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own — true, but not the fullest answer. Their specific granules stain differently (neutrophilic, eosinophilic/acidophilic, or basophilic/metachromatic), but again this is only one criterion among those listed.
explanations.D: Correct. Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils are grouped together as the granular leukocytes, but told apart from one another by three independent features held at once: the shape of their nucleus, their relative percentage of the total leukocyte count, and how their specific granules take up stain. A student who checks only one of the three risks misidentifying a cell whose other two features would have settled the call.

questions.learning_objective: State the three criteria — nuclear shape, percentage, granule staining — that distinguish the granular leukocytes.

questions.title: Which maturation stage is mainly acidophilic
questions.question: Which of the following cells have mainly acidophilic cytoplasm?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The proerythroblast is the earliest stage, with deeply basophilic (ribosome-rich) cytoplasm, not acidophilic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Erythroblast" alone is too general — cytoplasmic staining shifts across the erythroblast series from basophilic toward acidophilic, so the stage matters.
explanations.C: Correct. The orthochromatophilic erythroblast is the last nucleated stage before the reticulocyte, and by this stage haemoglobin has almost fully replaced the ribosomal machinery that made the earlier stages basophilic. Its cytoplasm therefore stains mainly acidophilic — the name "orthochromatophilic" literally marks it as having reached the normal (haemoglobin-dominant) staining pattern of a mature red cell's precursor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The basophilic erythroblast is named for the opposite property — deeply basophilic cytoplasm from its abundant ribosomes, not acidophilic staining.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the orthochromatophilic erythroblast as the maturation stage with mainly acidophilic cytoplasm.

questions.title: Which marrow is active
questions.question: The active bone marrow is:

explanations.A: Correct. Bone marrow is classified as active red marrow, which is actively haemopoietic and rich in developing blood cells, or inactive yellow marrow, which is largely replaced by fat and does not normally produce blood cells. Red marrow predominates in the flat bones and the ends of long bones in adults, while yellow marrow fills most of the long-bone shafts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Yellow marrow is the inactive form — its haemopoietic tissue has been largely replaced by fat cells, so it is not the active marrow this question asks for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "White marrow" is not a recognised marrow classification in this scheme; marrow is classified as red (active) or yellow (inactive).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Red is the correct listed answer, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that active bone marrow is red marrow, as distinct from inactive yellow marrow.

questions.title: Which precursor has no granules
questions.question: Which of the following have no granules?

explanations.A: Incorrect. By the metamyelocyte stage the cell already carries specific granules, having passed through the promyelocyte and myelocyte stages.
explanations.B: Correct. The myeloblast is the earliest recognisable stage of the granulocyte series: a large cell with a pale, finely stippled nucleus, prominent nucleoli, and a narrow rim of basophilic cytoplasm that carries no specific granules yet. Specific (secondary) granules first appear at the next stage, the promyelocyte, alongside the non-specific azurophilic granules that stage is known for, and specific granules then predominate from the myelocyte stage onward.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The promyelocyte already carries large non-specific azurophilic granules, one stage past the granule-free myeloblast.
explanations.D: Incorrect. By the myelocyte stage the cell has specific granules — this is in fact the stage named for actively producing them.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the myeloblast as the earliest granulocyte precursor, carrying no specific granules.

questions.title: Cell found only in bone marrow
questions.question: Found only in bone marrow:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pericytes sit around small blood vessels throughout the body, not only in bone marrow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Astrocytes are glial cells of the central nervous system and are not found in bone marrow at all.
explanations.C: Correct. The megakaryocyte, a distinctively large (50-70 micrometre) cell with a single very large multilobed nucleus and basophilic cytoplasm from which platelets detach, is found only in the bone marrow. It is one of the two cell types, along with the marrow's fat cells, used to identify a section as bone marrow rather than another tissue. Pericytes, astrocytes and myocytes are all found in other tissues throughout the body, so none of them serves as a bone-marrow-specific identifier the way the megakaryocyte does.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myocytes (muscle cells) are found in muscle tissue, not in bone marrow.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the megakaryocyte as a cell found only in bone marrow, used to identify a marrow section.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IHI-103 > Blood and Hemopoiesis > Bone marrow and hemopoiesis

questions.title: Definition of leukocytosis
questions.question: Leukocytosis is:

explanations.A: Correct. Leukocytosis is a raised total white-cell (leukocyte) count on the CBC, above the normal range of roughly 4,000-10,000 cells/mm3, most often from infection or malignancy. It is a CBC finding, not a clinical diagnosis on its own — the specific cause still has to be worked out from the rest of the clinical picture.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An increase in the red-cell count is polycythaemia, not leukocytosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A decrease in the white-cell count is leukopenia, the opposite of leukocytosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A decrease in the red-cell count is a form of anaemia, unrelated to leukocytosis.

questions.learning_objective: Define leukocytosis as a raised total white-cell count on the CBC.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IHI-103 > Blood and Hemopoiesis > Blood cells

questions.title: Origin of lymphocyte stem cells
questions.question: The stem cells of T & B-lymphocytes originate in the:

explanations.A: Correct. Like every other blood-cell line, T- and B-lymphocytes trace back to a common haemopoietic stem cell that originates in the bone marrow. B-lymphocytes complete their maturation there; T-lymphocyte precursors leave the marrow while still immature and complete their maturation in the thymus, but the stem cell both lines start from is a bone-marrow cell in both cases.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lymph node is a site where mature lymphocytes circulate and encounter antigen, not the site their stem cells originate from.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spleen, like the lymph node, is a peripheral lymphoid organ where mature lymphocytes reside and respond to antigen, not the origin of their stem cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The thymus is where immature T-lymphocyte precursors complete their later maturation, after leaving the bone marrow — it is a maturation site, not the origin of the stem cell itself, and it plays no role at all in B-lymphocyte development.

questions.learning_objective: State that the stem cells of both T- and B-lymphocytes originate in the bone marrow.

questions.title: RBC maturation changes, EXCEPT
questions.question: Changes occurring during maturation of RBCs are all EXCEPT:

options.D: Mitochondria and other cell organelles gradually disappear

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Cell size does decrease progressively across the erythroblast-to-erythrocyte maturation series.
explanations.B: Correct — this is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. The nucleus does become smaller and progressively condensed (heterochromatic) as the erythroblast matures, but it is never lobulated: at the orthochromatophilic-erythroblast stage the condensed nucleus is extruded from the cell whole. Lobulation is a granulocyte-only nuclear change (seen in neutrophils, for example), not a feature of erythroid maturation.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Ribosomal (basophilic) cytoplasm does fall as haemoglobin content rises across the series, which is also why cytoplasmic staining shifts from basophilic toward acidophilic.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Mitochondria and the other organelles are progressively lost, leaving the mature erythrocyte with no nucleus, no mitochondria and no ribosomes at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that RBC nuclear maturation condenses and extrudes the nucleus, and never lobulates it.

questions.title: Megakaryocyte facts (5-option)
questions.question: Megakaryocytes:

options.D: Are located mainly in the spleen

explanations.A: Incorrect. A megakaryocyte has one large nucleus that is polyploid (multiple sets of chromosomes within a single nucleus from repeated endomitosis), not several separate nuclei — it is not truly multinuclear.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Megakaryocytes are the precursors of platelets, not of macrophages; platelets detach from the megakaryocyte's cytoplasm via demarcation membranes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Megakaryocytes are polyploid, carrying multiple sets of chromosomes, not haploid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bone-marrow megakaryocytes are located in the bone marrow, not mainly in the spleen.
explanations.E: Correct. Every specific claim offered is wrong: megakaryocytes have one polyploid nucleus rather than being truly multinuclear, they are platelet precursors rather than macrophage precursors, they are polyploid rather than haploid, and they are bone-marrow (not splenic) cells. With all four specific options individually false, "none of the above" is the only correct answer.

questions.learning_objective: Rule out common misconceptions about megakaryocytes: not multinuclear, not macrophage precursors, not haploid, not splenic.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IHI-103 > Blood and Hemopoiesis > Bone marrow and hemopoiesis

questions.title: Which stromal cell stimulates hemopoiesis
questions.question: It stimulates the stem cell to form blood cell:

explanations.A: Correct. Bone-marrow reticular cells are stellate stromal cells that secrete the reticular fibre meshwork the developing blood cells sit on. Alongside that structural role, they provide the local growth-factor signal that stimulates haemopoietic stem cells to proliferate and differentiate into the various blood cell lines. This functional, stem-cell-stimulating role is distinct from — but sits alongside — the reticular cell's fibre-secreting structural role.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The fibroblast is the analogous cell of connective tissue proper elsewhere in the body, but the stimulating cell of the marrow stroma specifically is the reticular cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Marrow macrophages phagocytose debris and expelled erythroblast nuclei, but stimulating stem cells to differentiate is the reticular cell's role, not the macrophage's.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteogenic cells build bone tissue itself; they are not the cell responsible for stimulating haemopoietic stem cells in the marrow stroma.

questions.learning_objective: State that bone-marrow reticular cells stimulate haemopoietic stem cells to form blood cells.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IHI-103 > Blood and Hemopoiesis > Bone marrow and hemopoiesis

questions.title: Local fuel reserve for hemopoiesis
questions.question: Is the local fuel for hematopoiesis:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The reticular cell's role in the marrow stroma is stimulating stem-cell differentiation, not serving as the local fuel reserve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The fibroblast is not a normal component of bone-marrow stroma in the way the fat cell, reticular cell and macrophage are.
explanations.C: Correct. Fat cells (adipocytes) make up a large part of the bone-marrow stroma and, functionally, serve as its local energy reserve: the lipid they store is drawn on as fuel for the metabolically demanding process of hemopoiesis happening around them. They are also among the largest cells in the marrow, which is a separate identifying feature from this functional one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteogenic cells are concerned with building bone tissue, not with providing a local energy reserve for hemopoiesis.

questions.learning_objective: State that bone-marrow fat cells serve as the local fuel reserve for hemopoiesis.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IHI-103 > Blood and Hemopoiesis > Bone marrow and hemopoiesis

questions.title: Basophil statements, EXCEPT
questions.question: The following statements about the basophils are correct EXCEPT:

options.A: Form about 0,5% of the total leukocytic count

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Basophils are the rarest leukocyte, normally making up about 0.5% of the total leukocyte count.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Basophils, alongside neutrophils and eosinophils, are one of the three granular leukocytes.
explanations.C: Correct — this is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. The basophil's nucleus is bilobed or S-shaped, like the eosinophil's. It is also usually obscured by the cell's own numerous granules, rather than being simply "central and rounded" — a rounded nucleus is a feature of a monocyte or lymphocyte, not a basophil.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Basophils carry coarse, deeply basophilic (metachromatic with toluidine blue) specific granules — this is in fact the feature the cell is named for.

questions.learning_objective: State that the basophil nucleus is bilobed/S-shaped and usually obscured by granules, not simply rounded.

questions.title: Why the reticulocyte is named for a reticulum
questions.question: The name of the reticulocytes is due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Golgi complex is unrelated to the reticulocyte's name; the reticulocyte has already lost its Golgi by the time it is anucleate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nucleoli belong to nucleated cells; the anucleate reticulocyte has none.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a distinct organelle unrelated to the reticulocyte's naming.
explanations.D: Correct. A reticulocyte is visible as such only under a supravital stain (e.g. brilliant cresyl blue applied to living cells outside the body): the dye precipitates the cell's residual ribosomal RNA (polyribosomes left over from its erythroblast stage) into a stainable reticulum, or network, which is what gives the reticulocyte its name. This reticulum disappears as the cell fully matures into an erythrocyte, and it is not visible at all on an ordinary (non-supravital) blood film.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that the reticulocyte's reticulum is residual ribosomal RNA, visible only under supravital staining.

questions.title: Megakaryocyte facts (4-option)
questions.question: Megakaryocytes are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A megakaryocyte has a single large polyploid nucleus, not multiple separate nuclei.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Megakaryocytes are polyploid (multiple chromosome sets in one nucleus from repeated endomitosis), not haploid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Megakaryocytes are precursors of platelets, not of macrophages.
explanations.D: Correct. Megakaryocytes are not truly multinucleated (they carry one large polyploid nucleus), are polyploid rather than haploid, and are precursors of platelets, not of macrophages. As in the fuller version of this same question, every specific option offered here is individually false, so "none of the above" is the correct answer.

questions.learning_objective: Rule out common misconceptions about megakaryocytes: not multinucleated, not haploid, not macrophage precursors.

questions.title: Neutrophil identifying feature
questions.question: Neutrophils are characterized by one of the following:

options.A: Form 5-10% of the total leukocytic count

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neutrophils normally make up the large majority of leukocytes (roughly 60-70%), far above the 5-10% offered here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Metachromatic granule staining is the basophil's feature; neutrophil specific granules stain neutrally, not metachromatically.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neutrophils are granular leukocytes, carrying specific (neutrophilic) granules — they are not agranular.
explanations.D: Correct. The neutrophil's single nucleus is divided into three to five connected lobes. This is its most reliable identifying feature on a blood film, and it distinguishes the neutrophil at a glance from the other granulocytes and from mononuclear leukocytes such as monocytes and lymphocytes.

questions.learning_objective: State that the neutrophil's nucleus is multilobed (3-5 lobes).
questions.module_subject: O6U-IHI-103 > Blood and Hemopoiesis > Granulocyte identification

questions.title: Eosinophil identifying feature
questions.question: Eosinophils are characterized by one of the following:

options.B: Form 25% of the total leukocytic count

explanations.A: Correct. Eosinophils are identified by coarse specific granules that stain strongly acidophilic (eosin pink). On electron microscopy these granules show a dense crystalline core, a granule structure unique among the granulocytes to the eosinophil. This bilobed-nucleus, crystalline-granule combination is the eosinophil's most reliable identifying feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Eosinophils normally make up only about 1-4% of the total leukocyte count, far below the 25% offered here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The eosinophil's nucleus is bilobed, not simply rounded — a rounded nucleus belongs to a monocyte or lymphocyte.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Eosinophils are a distinct myeloid-lineage granulocyte; they are not converted into plasma cells, which arise instead from B-lymphocytes.

questions.learning_objective: State that eosinophils are identified by acidophilic, crystalline-cored specific granules.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IHI-103 > Blood and Hemopoiesis > Granulocyte identification

questions.title: Monocyte identifying feature
questions.question: Monocytes are characterized by one of the following:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Monocytes are agranular — they carry no specific granules, unlike the neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.
explanations.B: Correct. The monocyte's defining function is phagocytosis: it circulates briefly in an agranular, kidney-nucleated form before migrating into tissues and differentiating into a macrophage, which then phagocytoses pathogens and debris. This phagocytic role is the feature that most reliably characterises the monocyte-macrophage line.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Monocytes are a separate, myeloid-lineage cell; they are not the precursor of lymphocytes, which arise from their own lymphoid stem-cell lineage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A prominent (not negative) Golgi image is typical of an actively secreting protein-forming cell such as a plasma cell, not a defining feature used to characterise monocytes.

questions.learning_objective: State that the monocyte is agranular and phagocytic, and is not the precursor of lymphocytes.
